title: Electric Current & Resistance
summary: Electric current is the rate charge flows, $I = Q/t$ (amperes). In many materials current and voltage obey Ohm's law $V = IR$; resistance depends on the material and shape, $R = \rho L/A$; and electrical power is $P = IV = I^2R = V^2/R$. (University Physics Vol. 2, Ch. 9.)

current.plain: The rate that electric charge flows past a point.
current.in_class: $I = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}$, measured in amperes; direction is that of positive charge flow.

ampere.plain: The unit of electric current — one coulomb of charge per second.

resistance.plain: How strongly a material opposes the flow of current.
resistance.in_class: $R = V/I$, measured in ohms; larger $R$ means less current for the same voltage.

ohm.plain: The unit of resistance — one volt per ampere.

resistivity.plain: A material property saying how much it resists current, regardless of shape.
resistivity.in_class: $R = \rho\dfrac{L}{A}$: longer or thinner wires have more resistance.

Ohm's law.plain: For many materials, current is proportional to the voltage across them.
Ohm's law.in_class: $V = IR$ — the workhorse relation for resistors in this chapter.

drift velocity.plain: The slow average speed charges actually move through a wire.
drift velocity.in_class: Tiny (mm/s), even though the electrical signal travels near light speed.

power.plain: The rate energy is delivered or used.
power.in_class: $P = IV = I^2 R = V^2/R$, measured in watts.

concept_sections.heading: What current is
concept_sections.explanation: Electric current is how fast charge flows past a point: $I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$, measured in amperes (1 A = 1 C/s). By convention, current points the way positive charge would move — opposite to the actual electron flow in a wire.

concept_sections.heading: The microscopic picture
concept_sections.explanation: Inside a wire, countless electrons drift slowly (millimeters per second) under an applied field. The current relates to this drift by $I = nqv_d A$, where $n$ is the charge-carrier density and $v_d$ the drift speed. The 'signal' travels near light speed even though individual electrons crawl.

concept_sections.heading: Ohm's law
concept_sections.explanation: For an ohmic material the current is proportional to the voltage across it: $V = IR$. The constant $R$ is the resistance, in ohms ($\Omega$). More voltage pushes more current; more resistance allows less. Rearrange as needed: $I = V/R$ or $R = V/I$.

concept_sections.heading: What sets the resistance
concept_sections.explanation: Resistance grows with length and shrinks with cross-section: $R = \rho\dfrac{L}{A}$, where $\rho$ is the material's resistivity (copper is tiny, rubber is huge). A long thin wire resists more than a short fat one of the same material — just like a narrow pipe resists water flow.

concept_sections.heading: Electric power
concept_sections.explanation: Charge moving through a voltage delivers energy at rate $P = IV$. Using Ohm's law this is also $P = I^2R = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$. In a resistor this power becomes heat (a toaster, a bulb filament). Energy used is power times time; utilities bill it in kilowatt-hours.

real_world_examples.title: A fuse or circuit breaker
real_world_examples.scenario: Too many appliances trip the breaker.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Each device draws current $I = P/V$. When the total exceeds the breaker's rating, $I^2R$ heating in the wires would become unsafe, so the breaker opens the circuit.

real_world_examples.title: A light-bulb filament
real_world_examples.scenario: An incandescent bulb glows when switched on.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The thin, high-resistance filament dissipates $P = V^2/R$ as heat and light. Its small area $A$ and long coiled length $L$ give the large $R$ needed to reach glowing temperature.

real_world_examples.title: A warm extension cord
real_world_examples.scenario: A long thin cord feels warm under heavy load.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The cord's own resistance $R = \rho L/A$ dissipates $I^2R$. A longer or thinner cord has more $R$, so it wastes more power as heat — why heavy loads need thick cords.

problems.prompt: A charge of $60$ C passes a point in $30$ s. Find the current.
problems.hint: Current is charge per unit time.

problems.prompt: A $6.0\ \Omega$ resistor carries $2.0$ A. Find the voltage across it.
A device draws $3.0$ A at $12$ V. Find its resistance.
A copper wire ($\rho = 1.7\times10^{-8}\ \Omega\cdot\text{m}$) is $10$ m long with cross-section $1.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2$. Find its resistance.
A motor runs at $120$ V drawing $0.50$ A. Find its power.
A $10\ \Omega$ resistor carries $2.0$ A. Find the power dissipated.
How much energy (in J) does a $100$ W bulb use in $2.0$ hours?
problems.hint: Convert hours to seconds, then $E = Pt$.

problems.prompt: A $1500$ W heater runs on $120$ V. Find the current it draws and its resistance.
problems.hint: First get $I$ from $P = IV$, then $R = V/I$.

problems.prompt: How many electrons per second flow in a $2.0$ A current?
problems.hint: Each electron carries charge $e$; divide the current by $e$.

problems.prompt: A wire has resistance $2.0\ \Omega$. If it is stretched to twice its length with half the cross-sectional area, find the new resistance.
solution_steps: $R = \rho L/A$. Doubling $L$ multiplies $R$ by 2; halving $A$ multiplies by another 2.
problems.hint: See how $R = \rho L/A$ scales with each change.
